strengths: Novel and well-motivated architecture combining continuous-time event inference (EPDE), a lognormal mixture sampling process (MELP), and a biophysically-inspired dLIF prior to move beyond black-box EEG classifiers toward physiologically interpretable latent dynamics.

Solid theoretical contributions: a tractable IVP-based upper bound for an otherwise intractable path-measure KL divergence (Theorem 4.1), and a Lipschitz-based stability analysis of the inferred event-relational graph under lag perturbations (Theorem A.1/Corollary A.2), with full proofs provided.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning a controlled synthetic benchmark (with known ground-truth event rates/boundaries) and two real AD EEG cohorts, plus ablations isolating the contribution of the dLIF and ERG priors.

Interpretability-oriented visualizations (per-channel dLIF-inferred frequency shifts across AD/MCI/HC, and event-relational connectivity graphs vs. Pearson correlation) that qualitatively align with established EEG slowing and connectivity findings in AD literature.

Thorough appendix with architecture diagrams, pseudocode, computational cost comparisons, and additional metrics (sensitivity/specificity/AUC), which aids reproducibility despite no explicit code release mentioned.
weaknesses: The real-world AD cohorts are small and highly imbalanced (e.g., Cohort B has only 7 MCI subjects out of 168), and reported standard deviations are extremely large (e.g., baseline accuracy std of ±26% on Cohort B), yet no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests across folds) is provided to support claims that LERD 'consistently outperforms' baselines; several accuracy/F1 gaps are within one standard deviation of the strongest baseline.

LERD achieves the lowest AUC (0.838) among all compared models on Cohort B despite having the best accuracy/F1/sensitivity — this inconsistency is not discussed or explained, raising concerns about calibration, threshold sensitivity, or possible cherry-picking of metrics for the headline comparison.

The synthetic IoU comparison (Table 1) may be structurally biased in LERD's favor: baseline models (NODE, ODE-RNN, STRODE) have no explicit discrete 'event' output analogous to LERD's inferred events, so an IoU of exactly 0.000 for all three baselines across all bands looks more like a definitional artifact of the metric than a meaningful demonstration of a modeling failure, weakening the strength of this comparison.

On real EEG data there is no ground truth for latent events or edges, so validation of the 'physiology-aligned' claims rests entirely on qualitative visual agreement with known AD EEG slowing/connectivity phenomena (Figs. 2–3) rather than quantitative validation against independent biomarkers (e.g., MMSE scores, which are available for Cohort B but unused for this purpose).

The model has many interacting hyperparameters (λLIF, β, K mixture components, α edge slope, σ, dLIF gating) but the paper provides only a single ablation (presence/absence of the two priors) without sensitivity analysis over these hyperparameters, making it hard to judge robustness or reproducibility of the reported gains.

The theoretical results, while correctly derived, are relatively standard applications of change-of-variables/Lipschitz arguments; their practical impact on the tightness of the bound used in training (fixed small ε in Uε) is not empirically characterized (e.g., how tight is the bound in practice, how sensitive is training to ε).

strengths: The paper proposes a technically interesting framework (EPDE + MELP + dLIF prior + STDP-inspired ERG) that attempts to move beyond black-box EEG classifiers toward an interpretable, event-driven generative model, which is a worthwhile direction.

Reasonably thorough theoretical appendix, including an IVP-based tractable upper bound on an otherwise intractable path-measure KL and a Lipschitz-based stability bound for the inferred event-relational graph under lag perturbations.
Extensive appendix detailing architecture, training hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, computational cost, and pseudocode, which aids reproducibility.

Ablation study (Table 3) isolating the dLIF and ERG prior contributions, and qualitative visualizations (Figures 2-4) that are broadly consistent with known EEG slowing/connectivity-loss phenomena in AD.
Comparison against a reasonably comprehensive and current set of baselines (EEGNet, LSTM, ATCNet, ADFormer, LEAD, LCADNet).
weaknesses: Dataset AD Cohort B contains only 7 MCI subjects out of 168 participants; under 5-fold cross-subject CV this leaves roughly 1-2 MCI subjects per test fold, making the reported multi-class performance on this cohort statistically unreliable and the associated claims about 'subtler distinctions' largely unsupported.

A striking and unexplained inconsistency appears in Table 5/6: LERD achieves the best accuracy and sensitivity on Cohort B but a substantially *lower* AUC (0.8383) than nearly every baseline (up to 0.9714 for ADFormer). This is a serious red flag suggesting threshold-dependent or calibration artifacts, and it is not discussed anywhere in the main text, undermining the central claim that LERD 'consistently outperforms' baselines.

In the toy dataset (Table 1), NODE and ODE-RNN report an identical, degenerate 'Median Rate' of exactly 1.000 with a zero-width 95% CI across all three distinct frequency bands ([5-10],[10-15],[15-20] Hz). This strongly suggests either a broken/uninformative baseline implementation or an evaluation protocol/metric that is not meaningfully applicable to these models, casting doubt on the fairness of the comparison and the resulting IoU=0.000 conclusions used to motivate LERD.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests across folds) is reported anywhere despite large and overlapping standard deviations between LERD and the strongest baselines (e.g., LEAD, ADFormer) on Cohort A, making it unclear whether the reported improvements are meaningful rather than noise.

The physiology-alignment claims (Figure 2 frequency slowing, Figure 3 connectivity sparsification) are presented only as qualitative KDE/chord-diagram visualizations without any quantitative statistical group comparison (e.g., effect sizes, p-values), and are to some degree an expected consequence of the dLIF/Fisher-z regularizers built into the model rather than independent validation.

The theoretical stability result (Appendix A) is a fairly standard Lipschitz-composition argument for the chosen exponential edge kernel; while correct, it is somewhat oversold in the main text as a general 'stability guarantee for the inferred relational dynamics' when it is essentially a straightforward consequence of the kernel choice.

The classification task setup (binary vs. multi-class, and which specific class pairs are being distinguished per cohort) is not clearly specified in the main text for Table 2, making the reported accuracy/F1 numbers difficult to interpret precisely.
No statement about code or data release is provided, which limits practical reproducibility despite the detailed architectural appendix.

The synthetic validation task (single sinusoid plus Gaussian noise, single events per sequence of only 20 points) is quite simplistic relative to the complexity of real multichannel EEG dynamics claimed to be captured by the model, limiting how much the synthetic results can be used to support claims about real AD EEG data.

strengths: Novel, well-motivated integration of ideas: an event-driven continuous-time posterior (EPDE), a flexible stochastic inter-event model (MELP), and a biophysically-inspired dLIF prior, coupled with an STDP-motivated event-relational graph (ERG), applied to EEG-based dementia classification. This moves beyond black-box classifiers toward models with interpretable latent structure.

Solid theoretical contributions: a tractable IVP-based upper bound for the otherwise intractable path-measure KL divergence between the EPDE posterior and the dLIF renewal-process prior (Theorem 4.1), and an entry-wise/Frobenius stability bound for the inferred ERG under lag perturbations (Theorem A.1), both with complete proofs in the appendix.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: a controlled synthetic benchmark with known generative event rates (showing LERD recovers meaningful IoU structure while NODE/ODE-RNN/STRODE baselines collapse to IoU=0), plus two real AD EEG cohorts with cross-subject 5-fold evaluation and comparisons against several modern baselines (EEGNet, LCADNet, LSTM, ATCNet, ADFormer, LEAD).
Useful ablation study isolating the contribution of the dLIF prior and ERG prior separately and jointly, showing consistent (if not uniformly monotonic) benefits.

Qualitative visualizations (dLIF-inferred frequency slowing across AD/MCI/HC, ERG vs. Pearson connectivity patterns) are consistent with well-established EEG slowing and connectivity-reduction phenomena in AD/FTD literature, lending some face validity to the latent summaries.

Good reproducibility effort in the appendix: detailed architecture/shape tables, training hyperparameters, computational cost (FLOPs/params) comparison, and full pseudocode for MELP sampling, ODE evolution, and end-to-end training/inference.
weaknesses: The two real-world datasets are small (88 and 168 subjects) with severe class imbalance in Cohort B (only 7 MCI subjects), and standard deviations across folds are very large for several baselines (e.g., ±26% accuracy for EEGNet on Cohort B). No statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests across folds) is reported to support the claim that LERD's improvements are meaningful rather than within-noise.

A notable internal inconsistency: on Cohort B, LERD achieves the highest accuracy and sensitivity but the lowest AUC (0.838) among all compared models, most of which exceed 0.94 AUC. This discrepancy between accuracy and AUC is not discussed or explained, and raises concerns about threshold/calibration effects or possible evaluation issues that undermine confidence in the headline results.

The dLIF prior is explicitly described as "phenomenological," and while this honesty is appreciated, no quantitative validation is offered connecting inferred latent rates to independently measured spectral/oscillatory quantities (e.g., classical band-power slowing) on the same data; the frequency-shift figures are presented only qualitatively.

The toy/synthetic benchmark, while useful for sanity-checking event recovery, is a fairly simple sinusoidal-plus-Poisson-event generative process; it is unclear how well conclusions transfer to realistic multichannel EEG with mixing, artifacts, and non-stationary noise, and the IoU metric's construction (ground-truth 'boundaries' from a continuous rate parameter) is not fully specified in the main text.

No cross-cohort generalization experiment (e.g., train on Cohort A, test on Cohort B) is reported, despite the paper's framing around clinically useful, generalizable EEG diagnosis; all evaluations are within-cohort cross-subject folds only.
The paper does not mention code/data release, which limits independent reproducibility despite the detailed architectural appendix.

The ablation results are not uniformly monotonic (e.g., on Cohort B the ERG-only variant achieves higher F1 than the dual-prior model), which is not discussed, leaving some ambiguity about whether the two priors are truly complementary or partially redundant.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel synthesis for EEG-based AD analysis: an annotation-free Bayesian framework (EPDE + MELP + dLIF + ERG) that jointly infers latent event times, stochastic inter-event intervals, and event-lag relational graphs under a single variational objective, rather than treating EEG classification as a black-box mapping.

Provides non-trivial theoretical grounding: a tractable IVP-based representation for the otherwise intractable path-measure KL against the dLIF prior (Theorem 4.1), plus Lipschitz/concentration-based stability bounds for the inferred event-relational graph under lag perturbations, with full proofs in the appendix.

The paper is careful and explicit about the limits of its biological claims (dLIF is 'phenomenological,' ERG is a 'sensor-space, timing-derived' summary rather than source-level effective connectivity or synaptic plasticity), which is a responsible and clearly-articulated framing rarely found in similarly-scoped EEG deep learning papers.

Empirical evaluation spans a controlled synthetic benchmark (with known latent boundaries enabling IoU-based structural recovery, where LERD is the only method with non-zero IoU against NODE/ODE-RNN/STRODE) and two real multi-class AD EEG cohorts under a strict subject-level cross-validation protocol, together with ablations (Table 4), auxiliary-weight sensitivity sweeps (Appendix E.5), and computational-cost reporting (FLOPs/params, Table 5), reflecting a fairly thorough evaluation effort.

Qualitative/quantitative visualizations (dLIF-derived frequency slowing across 19/19 EEG channels, HC/FTD/AD connectivity graphs) are broadly consistent with well-established AD EEG phenomenology (oscillatory slowing, reduced connectivity), lending some external plausibility to the recovered latent structures beyond raw classification numbers.
weaknesses: The only setting with ground-truth latent structure (toy dataset) uses a very simple sinusoidal generative process with exponential inter-event times; recovered IoU values are still modest in absolute terms (0.2–0.47), so it is unclear how well the model's claimed 'accurate latent event recovery' would transfer to the qualitatively more complex, non-stationary dynamics of real EEG, where no ground truth exists to validate the inferred events/graphs directly.

Real-data classification gains over strong baselines are often within, or close to, one standard deviation (e.g., Table 2 Cohort A: LERD 75.03±8.29 vs. LEAD 72.68±4.57; Cohort B F1: LERD 64.87±10.67 vs. ADFormer 63.89±12.09), and no paired statistical significance tests (e.g., per-fold paired t-test or Wilcoxon) are reported, making it hard to be confident the improvements are not within noise, especially given the small, class-imbalanced cohorts (only 7 MCI subjects in Cohort B).

Metric behavior is internally inconsistent in places: LERD achieves the highest accuracy/F1 on Cohort B but has a notably lower AUC (0.8383) than several baselines with AUC >0.95 (Table 7), which is not discussed and raises questions about probability calibration or threshold sensitivity that could affect clinical interpretability claims.

The pipeline has substantial complexity (EPDE, MELP mixture with K components, dLIF gating, ERG mapping, GCN fusion) and many auxiliary hyperparameters (β, λ_LIF, σ, mixture components, ODE substeps); while a one-factor sensitivity sweep is provided, joint sensitivity/interaction effects and full hyperparameter selection protocol (e.g., how weights were tuned per dataset without leaking test information) are not fully detailed, which affects reproducibility confidence beyond the promised code release.

The theoretical contribution reuses a prior shift-stability lemma (Lemma A.1, credited to Huang et al. 2021/STRODE) and builds fairly directly on that line of continuous-time/stochastic-boundary modeling; while the IVP-KL derivation and ERG stability analysis are new applications, the conceptual novelty of the theory itself is incremental relative to existing point-process/Neural-ODE variational machinery.

Group-level dynamical claims (e.g., AD < MCI < HC frequency ordering in Figure 2, denser HC connectivity in Figure 3) are presented as consistent with literature but are not accompanied by formal statistical tests (e.g., permutation tests, effect sizes) comparing the groups' inferred rate/graph distributions, so the 'physiology-aligned' claims remain qualitative/descriptive rather than statistically validated.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually interesting unified framework (EPDE + MELP + dLIF prior + ERG) that tries to combine continuous-time event modeling, biophysically inspired priors, and relational graph inference in a single variational objective for EEG-based AD analysis, addressing a genuine gap between black-box classifiers and mechanistic interpretability.

Reasonably thorough theoretical treatment, including a tractable IVP-based surrogate for an otherwise intractable path-measure KL and a Lipschitz-based stability bound for the inferred event-relational graph under lag perturbations.

Experiments span synthetic data (with known latent structure) and two real AD EEG cohorts, with ablations over the dLIF/ERG priors, auxiliary-weight sensitivity sweeps, and qualitative visualizations (frequency slowing across HC/MCI/AD, graph sparsification) that broadly track established EEG-AD phenomenology.

The paper is unusually forthcoming about interpretive caveats (e.g., explicitly stating the dLIF prior is phenomenological, that ERG is a sensor-space timing summary rather than causal connectivity), which is a positive for honest limitations reporting.
weaknesses: A central soundness concern: on AD Cohort B, LERD reports the highest accuracy (89.82%) but a markedly lower AUC (0.8383) than every baseline (0.9486–0.9714, Table 7). Since AUC is more robust to the severe class imbalance in this cohort (only 7 MCI subjects among 168), this discrepancy strongly suggests the accuracy gains are driven by majority-class/majority-vote aggregation effects rather than genuinely superior discrimination, undermining the paper's central performance claims and is not adequately discussed or reconciled in the main text.

Real-world evaluation datasets are small and severely imbalanced (Cohort B has only 7 MCI subjects; Cohort A has 88 subjects total), and reported standard deviations for accuracy/F1 substantially overlap between LERD and the strongest baselines (e.g., Table 2: 75.03±8.29 vs LEAD 72.68±4.57), yet no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests across folds) is provided to support claims of consistent outperformance.

The synthetic-data validation of event/structure recovery (Table 1) shows all baselines get exactly IoU=0, but the paper itself explains this is because NODE/ODE-RNN 'do not natively output latent event boundaries' — i.e., the comparison is structurally unfair by design rather than a fair head-to-head test, weakening the strength of this evidence for LERD's claimed structural-recovery advantage. Even LERD's own IoU scores (0.20–0.47) are modest.

The physiology-alignment claims (e.g., dLIF frequency slowing HC>MCI>AD, denser HC connectivity graphs) are essentially confirmatory of well-established EEG findings that any reasonably trained AD/HC classifier would likely reproduce; they do not provide strong independent validation of the specific mechanistic machinery (EPDE/MELP/dLIF/ERG) beyond what a much simpler spectral analysis would show, so the claimed interpretability benefit over standard pipelines is not clearly demonstrated.

Ablations (Table 4) only toggle the two prior regularizers on/off; there is no ablation isolating whether the core event-based EPDE/MELP machinery itself (vs. a simpler encoder without explicit event modeling) is necessary for the observed classification gains, leaving the paper's key architectural novelty empirically under-supported.

The theoretical contributions, while correct, are somewhat modest in depth (a change-of-variables reformulation of a KL integral and a straightforward Lipschitz stability argument for an exponential edge map), and their practical necessity/impact versus simpler regularization choices is not clearly isolated in the ablations.

The manuscript's code-availability footnote is truncated/empty ('Our code is available at:'), leaving reproducibility of a fairly complex multi-module pipeline (EPDE, MELP, dLIF, ERG, GCN fusion) unverifiable from the paper alone, despite the extensive architectural appendix.

strengths: Novel and coherent unification of continuous-time event inference (EPDE), stochastic interval modeling (MELP), and an electrophysiology-inspired dLIF prior into a single annotation-free Bayesian framework for latent event and relational-graph discovery in multichannel EEG, addressing a genuine gap between black-box classifiers and mechanistic/interpretable models.

Solid theoretical contribution: a tractable IVP-based representation of the otherwise intractable path-measure KL between the EPDE posterior and the dLIF prior (Theorem 4.1), plus Lipschitz-based stability bounds (deterministic and Gaussian noise) for the inferred event-relational graph, both with full proofs in the appendix.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: a synthetic benchmark with known ground-truth event boundaries (showing LERD is the only compared method with non-trivial boundary IoU while matching or exceeding cosine similarity), plus two real AD/FTD/MCI EEG cohorts with a strict subject-level 5-fold cross-validation protocol and comparisons against 6 competitive baselines including transformer and foundation-model baselines (ADformer, LEAD).

Careful and honest framing of what the model does and does not claim: explicit statements that the dLIF component is phenomenological (not single-neuron), that the ERG is a sensor-space timing summary rather than source-level causal connectivity, and that Pearson-correlation regularization is weak and not meant to reproduce standard connectivity analysis.

Thorough ablations (prior components, one-factor auxiliary-weight sweeps) and physiologically consistent qualitative findings (inferred dLIF frequency shows HC > MCI > AD ordering in 18-19/19 channels), which lends some external validity to the latent summaries beyond raw classification accuracy.
Additional practical considerations addressed: computational cost/FLOPs comparison, per-window inference latency, and extended metrics (sensitivity/specificity/AUC) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Real-world evaluation is based on small and, in one cohort, highly imbalanced datasets (88 subjects in cohort A; 168 subjects but only 7 MCI subjects in cohort B), which the paper itself flags as a source of large fold-to-fold variance; this limits confidence in the generalizability of the reported gains, and no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests across folds) is provided to substantiate that LERD's improvements over the closest baselines (e.g., LEAD, ADformer) are not within noise, despite visibly overlapping standard deviations in Table 2.

Inconsistent secondary results undermine the overall narrative of improvement: on Cohort B, LERD achieves the highest accuracy but the lowest AUC (0.8383) among all compared methods (Table 7), a discrepancy that is not discussed or explained, raising concerns about threshold/majority-vote sensitivity versus genuine discriminative improvement.

The toy-dataset IoU values used to argue LERD recovers latent event structure are themselves fairly modest (0.20-0.47), and the zero-IoU baselines (NODE, ODE-RNN) are somewhat unfairly disadvantaged since they do not natively output event boundaries; while the paper acknowledges this, it still uses the comparison as a headline result supporting the model's core novelty claim.

The paper references shared code ('Our code is available at:') but the footnote link is empty/missing in the manuscript, undermining verifiability and reproducibility of the fairly complex multi-module pipeline (EPDE, MELP, dLIF, ERG, GCN, multiple regularizer weights).

The biophysical grounding of the dLIF prior remains a substantial conceptual stretch: mapping a single-compartment leaky-integrate-and-fire abstraction (designed for single-neuron spiking) onto population-level, sensor-space EEG rate dynamics is only loosely justified, and although the authors caveat this as 'phenomenological,' the paper still leans on this framing extensively (e.g., interpreting inferred 'firing rates' as characteristic EEG frequencies) without independent validation that these rates correspond to any established physiological quantity beyond correlation with known AD-related slowing.

Ablation and hyperparameter-sensitivity analyses (Table 4, Table 8) are conducted only on Cohort A, leaving open whether the same weight ranges and prior contributions transfer to Cohort B or other datasets.

The graph-connectivity comparison (Figure 3) is purely qualitative (visual density/sparsity), without any quantitative agreement or divergence metric between LERD's ERG and Pearson connectivity, or any validation against established AD connectivity literature beyond visual impression.
